records.quote:
And the rain beat on the
      dock-leaves to make drum-music for their sake, and the sun shone in order
      to give the burdock forest a color for their sakes; and they were very
      happy, and the whole family was happy; for they, indeed were so.
records.paraphrase: The snails believe the rain and sun exist for their benefit, a self-centered worldview presented for the reader to notice.

records.quote:
The old white snails were the first persons of distinction in the world,
      that they knew; the forest was planted for their sake, and the manor-house
      was there that they might be boiled and laid on a silver dish.
records.paraphrase: The snails regard themselves as the most important beings and believe the world exists for their sake, contrasting with the reader's knowledge.

records.quote:
I should like to know how far it extends, and what there is
      outside!
records.paraphrase: Mother Snail voices curiosity about the extent of the world and what lies beyond it.

records.quote:
they were never boiled, and never came on the silver
      dishes; so from this they concluded that the manor-house had fallen to
      ruins, and that all the men in the world were extinct; and as no one
      contradicted them, so, of course it was so.
records.paraphrase: From never being boiled, the snails infer that the manor-house is ruined and all humans are extinct, and their conclusion stands unchallenged.

records.quote:
I am very
      happy to think that we have our good house, and the little one has his
      also! There is more done for us than for all other creatures, sure enough;
      but can you not see that we are folks of quality in the world?
records.paraphrase: Mother Snail expresses satisfaction and a belief that the snails are privileged above all creatures.

candidate.quote:
Now, there was an old manor-house, where they no longer ate snails, they
      were quite extinct; but the burdocks were not extinct, they grew and grew
      all over the walks and all the beds; they could not get the mastery over
      them
      it was a whole forest of burdocks.
candidate.paraphrase: The custom of eating snails has ended and the garden has become an overgrown forest of burdocks.

quarantined.reason: quote could not be located in prepared story

candidate.quote:
There is nothing at all,
      said Father Snail. 
      No place can be better than
      ours, and I have nothing to wish for!
candidate.paraphrase: Father Snail insists there is nothing beyond their world and he desires nothing more.

criteria.rationale: The story is a fable about snails; it presents no scientific fact, theory, discovery, natural process, or speculative science in a material way. Mentions of rain and sun are decorative, not scientific content.
No device, technique, engineered system, or invention appears or affects the setting, problem, or outcome. The 'house' is the snail's shell, a natural feature, not an invention.
There is no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement. The tale unfolds in a vaguely present/former time with no time travel.

The snails reason from a premise (never being boiled) to a conclusion (the manor-house is ruined and humans are extinct). This is a flawed extrapolative inference used satirically, so its status as genuine consequence-development from an identifiable premise is uncertain.

Mother Snail voices curiosity about the world's extent, and the snails draw a conclusion from observed absence of boiling. This resembles observation and inference, but it is self-centered, unsystematic pseudo-reasoning that satirizes rather than materially demonstrates scientific method.
No other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors from them appear. The ants and gnats are ordinary garden creatures, not cosmic visitors.

The snails' belief that all humans are extinct is a mistaken, satirical inference presented ironically, not an actual, impending, or causally central large-scale disaster. No real catastrophe occurs or drives the narrative.

candidates.description: The snails' self-centered cosmology: a worldview in which the burdock forest was planted for their sake, humans exist to boil them onto silver dishes, and the rain and sun operate for their benefit. From the absence of being boiled they infer humanity's extinction and the ruin of the manor-house, and this belief becomes uncontested 'truth' in their storyworld.

novelty.rationale: The story is a satirical fable of anthropomorphized snails whose parochial self-importance mirrors human vanity. Nothing in the storyworld departs totalizingly from the authorial empirical norm; snails simply misinterpret an ordinary garden. The estranging force is allegorical/satirical rather than a world-altering material or social difference. There is no totalizing novum that changes the story universe.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The snails employ a quasi-inferential logic (from never being boiled they conclude humans are extinct) that is coherent and immanent, but it is a fallacy of parochial reasoning rather than a systematic imaginary science or social order. The talking-animal frame is a fabular convention closer to fantasy than to a cognitively validated estrangement.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The snails' self-centered worldview is the organizing principle of the entire tale, governing the marriage, the dialogue, and the closing inference of human extinction. It dominates the narrative logic.

estrangement.rationale: The reader perceives the gap between the snails' conviction that the forest and cosmos exist for their sake and the mundane reality of an overgrown abandoned garden, producing satirical estrangement about human self-importance.
